results.name: recency_minus_primacy_extrapolation
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples and targets outside the examples' [min,max] span, yes rate for targets strictly closer to the last-shown example minus yes rate for targets strictly closer to the first-shown one; observed above null means people generalize more around the most recent example than the order-blind model predicts (recency).
results.code:
# name: recency_minus_primacy_extrapolation
# description: For sets of 2+ examples and targets outside the examples' [min,max] span, yes rate for targets strictly closer to the last-shown example minus yes rate for targets strictly closer to the first-shown one; observed above null means people generalize more around the most recent example than the order-blind model predicts (recency).
def _m(y, m):
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    first = X[:, 0]
    last = X[np.arange(len(X)), n - 1]
    out = (n >= 2) & ((t < mn) | (t > mx))
    dl = np.abs(t - last)
    dfst = np.abs(t - first)
    return _m(y, out & (dl < dfst)) - _m(y, out & (dfst < dl))

results.name: round_target_nonexample_yes
results.description: Yes rate for targets that are multiples of 10 and not among the examples, on sets where not every example is a multiple of 10; observed below null means people reject round numbers more than the model predicts (round targets feel unrelated), above null means a round-number attraction.
results.code:
# name: round_target_nonexample_yes
# description: Yes rate for targets that are multiples of 10 and not among the examples, on sets where not every example is a multiple of 10; observed below null means people reject round numbers more than the model predicts (round targets feel unrelated), above null means a round-number attraction.
def _m(y, m):
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    allround = np.nansum(X % 10 == 0, axis=1) == n
    return _m(y, (t % 10 == 0) & (dist > 0) & ~allround)

results.name: single_example_gradient
results.description: For one-example sets, yes rate for targets 1-5 away minus yes rate for targets 6-20 away; observed above null means people's similarity gradient around a lone example is steeper than the model's (it over-generalizes at mid distance), below null shallower.

# description: For one-example sets, yes rate for targets 1-5 away minus yes rate for targets 6-20 away; observed above null means people's similarity gradient around a lone example is steeper than the model's (it over-generalizes at mid distance), below null shallower.
def _m(y, m):
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)

results.name: yes_carry_over
results.description: Within each participant (a new one starts at trial_index 0), yes rate on trials whose previous trial (a different set) was answered yes minus yes rate after a no; observed above null means responses perseverate/carry over across trials beyond what the stimulus-driven model predicts.
results.code:
# name: yes_carry_over
# description: Within each participant (a new one starts at trial_index 0), yes rate on trials whose previous trial (a different set) was answered yes minus yes rate after a no; observed above null means responses perseverate/carry over across trials beyond what the stimulus-driven model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()
    pid = np.cumsum(ti == 0)
    ok = np.zeros(len(y), bool)
    ok[1:] = (pid[1:] == pid[:-1]) & (s[1:] != s[:-1])
    prev = np.zeros(len(y))
    prev[1:] = y[:-1]
    a = ok & (prev == 1)
    b = ok & (prev == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(y[a].mean() - y[b].mean())

results.name: tight_cluster_outside_yes
results.description: For sets of 2+ examples spanning at most 10, yes rate for targets 1-5 outside the span minus yes rate for non-example targets inside it; observed above null means people blur the edges of tight clusters more (and/or fill them in less) than the size principle in the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: tight_cluster_outside_yes
# description: For sets of 2+ examples spanning at most 10, yes rate for targets 1-5 outside the span minus yes rate for non-example targets inside it; observed above null means people blur the edges of tight clusters more (and/or fill them in less) than the size principle in the model predicts.
def _m(y, m):
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    tight = (n >= 2) & (mx - mn <= 10)
    inside = (t >= mn) & (t <= mx) & (dist > 0)
    near_out = ((t < mn) | (t > mx)) & (dist <= 5)
    return _m(y, tight & near_out) - _m(y, tight & inside)

results.name: late_minus_early_yes
results.description: Yes rate on the second half of each session (trial_index >= half the maximum) minus the first half; observed above null means people grow more liberal over the session than the stationary model predicts (below null: more conservative).

results.name: far_out_of_span_yes
results.description: Yes rate for targets more than 15 beyond the examples' span (below min or above max) on sets of 2+ examples; observed above null means people keep extending to the number-line ends more than the open-ended-range discount allows (observed below null: the model still over-extends far).
results.code:
# name: far_out_of_span_yes
# description: Yes rate for targets more than 15 beyond the examples' span (below min or above max) on sets of 2+ examples; observed above null means people keep extending to the number-line ends more than the open-ended-range discount allows (observed below null: the model still over-extends far).
def _m(y, m):
    return float(y[m].mean()) if m.sum() > 0 else 0.0

def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(X), axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy().astype(float)
    y = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    mn = np.nanmin(X, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(X, axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(X - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    gap = np.maximum(mn - t, t - mx)
    return _m(y, (n >= 2) & (gap > 15))
